name: Stonehenge
info: A prehistoric megalithic monument on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, built in phases from about 3100 BC to about 1600 BC by a people without writing, and aligned on the solstice sunrise and sunset.

facts.made: Neolithic and Bronze Age communities of southern Britain, over at least 1,500 years; the builders of the first phases descended mainly from early farmers who reached Britain about 4000 BC, and the Bell Beaker people arrived during the megalithic phase
facts.form: A circular bank and ditch about 110 m across; an outer circle of sarsen uprights about 4 m high joined by lintels with mortise and tenon joints; five trilithons in a horseshoe; rings and settings of smaller bluestones from Wales
facts.where: Salisbury Plain, two miles west of Amesbury, Wiltshire; owned by the Crown Estate and managed by English Heritage, the surrounding land owned by the National Trust
facts.known: The solstice alignment; the sarsen circle and trilithons; bluestones brought from the Preseli Hills; the Aubrey holes and early cremation burials; the debate over its purpose; Merlin in Geoffrey of Monmouth's legend; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986

t: Stonehenge was built and rebuilt over some 1,500 years, from an earthwork of about 3100 BC to the sarsen circle of 2600 to 2400 BC and later rearrangements of the bluestones.
It was a place of burial from its beginnings, and its builders moved bluestones some 140 to 150 miles from the Preseli Hills in Wales.
Its purpose remains debated: an observatory, a place of healing, a domain of the dead linked to Durrington Walls, or a symbol of unity.
dyk: Cecil Chubb bought Stonehenge at auction in 1915 for £6,600, reportedly on a whim because he believed a local man should own it, and gave it to the nation three years later.
ev: The first monument, a circular bank and ditch with the ring of Aubrey holes, was dug
The builders abandoned timber for stone and set up bluestones in the centre of the site
The great circle of sarsen stones and the trilithon horseshoe were raised
The Y and Z Holes, the last known construction at the site, were dug
John Aubrey examined the site and recorded the pits that bear his name
The Ancient Monuments Protection Act made it a legally protected monument
Cecil Chubb bought the site at auction and gave it to the nation three years later
Stonehenge and its surroundings were added to the list of World Heritage Sites

sections.origins:
The site was used long before the monument. Four or possibly five large Mesolithic postholes dated to around 8000 BC held pine posts, three or four of them aligned east to west, and a possibly contemporary settlement has been found at Blick Mead, a spring a mile away. Analysis of mollusc shells suggests the builders took advantage of natural clearings in the woodland of Salisbury Plain. In the earlier Neolithic people built a causewayed enclosure at Robin Hood's Ball and long barrows nearby, and in about 3500 BC the Stonehenge Cursus was built 700 metres to the north as the first farmers cleared the trees.

DNA studies indicate that the builders of the first phases were closely related to Early and Middle Neolithic populations of Iberia and Central Europe, with about 75% ancestry from early farmers and 25% from Western Hunter-Gatherers; they reached Britain about 4000 BC. Cereal growing appears to have fallen out of favour between 3300 and 1500 BC, when most major phases were built. The Bell Beaker people arrived around 2500 BC, and over time more than 90% of Britain's Neolithic gene pool was replaced. The stones stand in the densest complex of Neolithic and Bronze Age monuments in England, with several hundred burial mounds.
sections.content:
The monument, now in ruins, consists of an outer ring of vertical sarsen stones, each around 4 metres high and weighing around 25 tons, topped by lintels held with mortise and tenon joints, a feature unique among contemporary monuments. Inside is a ring of smaller bluestones, and within these stand five trilithons, pairs of uprights joined by a lintel, in a horseshoe open to the north-east; the tallest, the Great Trilithon, would have been 7.3 metres high. The great trilithon, the horseshoe, the Heel Stone and the Avenue are aligned on the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset.

Around the stones runs a circular bank and ditch about 110 metres across, with a ring of 56 pits called the Aubrey holes. Outside the north-eastern entrance stands the Heel Stone, and the fallen Slaughter Stone is the last of the portal stones; four Station Stones and the Avenue, a pair of ditches and banks leading 3 kilometres to the River Avon, belong to the later phases. Carvings of a dagger and axeheads on the sarsens resemble Bronze Age weapons. The sarsens are silicified sandstone, the bluestones dolerite, tuff, rhyolite or sandstone.
sections.making:
The first monument, dated to around 3100 BC, was a bank and ditch dug in sections with antler picks; deer and ox bones and flint tools were placed in the ditch. The Aubrey holes may have held timbers or, as a recent excavation suggests, a first circle of bluestones. Between about 2900 and 2600 BC timber structures were added. Around 2600 BC the builders turned to stone and set up to 80 bluestones in the Q and R Holes. These were generally accepted to come from the Preseli Hills in Pembrokeshire; quarries at Craig Rhos-y-felin and elsewhere support transport by people rather than glaciers. Parker Pearson's team has argued that some came from a dismantled circle at Waun Mawn.

Between 2600 and 2400 BC some 30 sarsens were brought from West Woods, about 26 kilometres north, dressed and raised with woodworking joints; the uprights widen slightly towards the top and the lintels curve to follow the circle. Later phases rearranged the bluestones, until about 1930 to 1600 BC they formed a horseshoe. The Altar Stone's source remains unknown after a 2024 match with north-east Scotland was questioned in 2026. Experiments show that Neolithic methods could move such stones, as a 1995 sleigh trial with a 40-ton slab did.
sections.reception:
Its builders left no written records, and its uses are debated. It seems to have been a place of burial from its start: cremations from about 3000 BC lay in the Aubrey holes, and in its second phase it served as the earliest known cremation cemetery in the British Isles. Animal teeth at Durrington Walls, which Mike Parker Pearson thinks was the builders' camp, suggest that as many as 4,000 people gathered for midwinter and midsummer feasts. Parker Pearson sees Stonehenge as a domain of the dead joined by the Avon to a land of the living at Durrington Walls.

Gerald Hawkins argued in the 1960s that it was laid out to observe the Sun and Moon; Geoffrey Wainwright and Timothy Darvill proposed a place of healing. Roman-era coins, pottery and animal bones suggest ritual activity in that period, and a man beheaded between 600 and 690 AD was buried within the circles. Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th-century history told how Merlin brought the stones from Ireland. Inigo Jones thought it Roman, and John Aubrey and William Stukeley linked it to the Druids. Since 1905 Neo-druids and other modern pagans have gathered there.
sections.survival:
Until the 17th century stones were taken away for building, and in the 19th century tourists chipped off souvenirs. A trilithon fell in 1797 and stone 22 in a storm in 1900. William Gowland straightened and set a stone in concrete in 1901, and further restorations in 1958 and 1963 re-erected fallen sarsens on concrete bases. Excavators from William Cunnington and William Hawley to Richard Atkinson, Stuart Piggott and the Stonehenge Riverside Project of 2003 to 2008 have studied the site; Hawley exhumed the Aubrey hole cremations in 1920 and reburied them together in 1935.

Henry VIII's acquisition of Amesbury Abbey began a series of private owners, until Cecil Chubb bought the site in 1915 and gave it to the nation. A public subscription from 1927 bought the land around it, and the aerodrome beside it was cleared in the 1930s. Access has been contested: the Stonehenge Free Festival ran from 1972 to 1984 and ended with the Battle of the Beanfield in 1985, and solstice gatherings returned after a European Court of Human Rights ruling. The stones were roped off in 1977, a road beside them closed in 2013, and a planned road tunnel was abandoned in 2026.
sections.legacy:
Its name gave archaeology the word henge, used for circular banked enclosures with an internal ditch. The Oxford English Dictionary traces the name to Old English and to "stones supported in the air", while Christopher Chippindale offers hinge or hang as the root. It is one of the best-known landmarks in the United Kingdom and is regarded as a British cultural icon; it has been a scheduled monument since 1882 and part of a World Heritage Site since 1986.

Its legend spread through adaptations of Geoffrey of Monmouth in Wace, Layamon and the Welsh Brut y Brenhinedd, and folklore told of the Devil hurling the Heel Stone at a friar. Parker Pearson suggests the Merlin tale may hold "a grain of truth", since the bluestones probably came from Wales. The historian Ronald Hutton noted the irony that modern Druids arrived just as archaeologists were evicting the ancient Druids from it. Research continues: landscape surveys since 2010 have revealed many monuments and pits nearby, and the solstices still draw thousands of visitors to the stones, where English Heritage permits access at the solstices and equinoxes.

summary: Stonehenge is a prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain, built in phases from about 3100 BC to 1600 BC: an earthwork, rings of Welsh bluestones and a circle of great sarsens with lintels, aligned on the solstices. A place of burial from its beginnings, its purpose is still debated, and it is now a protected World Heritage Site and a place of modern pagan worship.
